analysis.title: Mid-term blues for a humbled President
key_insights: Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the US midterms, which the author calls a humbling defeat for the Trump administration. The author had been calling for this outcome but was still surprised by the scale.

Trump has acknowledged that the Middle East conflict contributed to the Party's defeat. Vance and Trump Jr. are reportedly seeking distance and pushing to end the conflict. Chatter suggests hawks such as Hegseth could be removed.
A material escalation in the Iran conflict is now seen as a tail risk rather than a dominant theme. A peace deal may still be difficult.

Even if the Middle East status quo continues, US inflation is expected to peak over the next few months and be back below 3% by mid-2027. The author still expects Warsh to hike in December and again in Q1, then hold. This is close to what markets discount, so a substantial yield rally is hard to project unless growth slows materially.

Democrat gains have triggered a material reversal in AI-related stocks. The author expects greater restrictions on AI infrastructure build-out but still sees business investment supporting GDP. A very material drop in equity valuations would be needed to tighten financial conditions enough to change Fed policy.

Recent price action is linked to hedge fund de-grossing and further pod closures. A regulatory-induced slowing of AI projects could make growth more sustainable and ease the supply of debt and equity issuance, so hyperscaler spreads may stabilise. The author is minded to add exposure to hyperscaler debt after being very sceptical for a year.
Robust US GDP is likely to slow CPI's return to the Fed's target. The author thinks a declining CPI path below 3% will satisfy Warsh and the FOMC, so hikes beyond Q1 should not be needed.

Eurozone CPI could peak at 4.5% in Q1 on elevated gas prices, then fall below 2% by this time next year as base effects reverse. The author thinks markets under-estimate the chance that the ECB hikes in December, holds, then eases before end-2027.

The author is constructive on European yields. If energy prices reverse, France and Italy, with the highest debt burdens, would benefit most. Investors are broadly short OAT, so the pain trade is spread narrowing, a tactical long. The author remains structurally more bearish on France.

The author thinks Eurozone sovereign spreads are wider than likely default rates justify, since a Eurozone break-up is unlikely. They added exposure in Italy and France and re-entered Romania at a spread above 300bp after a political compromise that may avert a downgrade.

The author is more constructive on gilts. Headline UK inflation may exceed 5% next spring, but without broadening price pressures the BoE may hike only once or twice more after raising rates to 4% at yesterday's MPC meeting.
UK politics: the risk of an early election remains. A Conservative victory probability could help gilts rally if PM Burnham does not turn too fiscally profligate.

EM: Venezuela and Argentina underperformed on Trump stumbles and read-across from Lula's Brazil victory. The author sees little read-across from Brazil to Argentina or other countries and still looks for a recovery in Brazilian assets, since Lula represents continuity.

FX volatility is low. The author closed a long US dollar position after the midterms, added Mexican peso exposure and sees value in several EM currencies on carry versus volatility. Softer energy prices should help the euro recover.

Credit: October saw widespread de-risking in credit hedge funds, so the technical backdrop is more constructive. The author is more inclined to add risk, favours moderately long risk into year-end as seasonals turn positive, and sees scope for euro credit to catch up. Spreads remain tied to equities and vulnerable to a flight to quality.

The Democrats could reach 56 Senate seats depending on Mississippi and Alaska, still 11 short of a majority to impeach. The author says the probability of Trump not completing his term has increased. DeSantis called the results a near 'extinction level event'.
The author expects a calmer investment landscape once the tech and AI moves play out, with yields and spreads more likely to fall than rise.
